insider_note: This whole method is just three steps in sequence — complete the square, name a, plug into the standard Tan⁻¹ formula — and every other question on this page uses the same three steps with a different quadratic.

steps.label: Complete the square in the denominator
steps.why: Adding and subtracting (1/2)² — half the coefficient of x, squared — rewrites the quadratic as a perfect square plus a constant, which is the only form the standard Tan⁻¹ formula accepts.
common_mistakes: Adding (1/2)² without also subtracting it, which changes the value of the expression.
Using half the coefficient of x² instead of half the coefficient of x.
steps.memory_tip: Half the x-coefficient, squared, added and subtracted — that pair never changes the expression's value.

steps.label: Identify the standard form and its constant a
lines: with x written as (x + 1/2) and a = √3/2
steps.why: Writing the constant 3/4 as a square (√3/2)² makes the match to the standard x² + a² pattern explicit, so the formula for ∫dx/(x²+a²) can be applied directly.
common_mistakes: Using a = 3/4 instead of a = √3/2 — a is the square ROOT of the constant, not the constant itself.
Forgetting that the ‘x’ in the standard formula is really (x + 1/2) here, not x alone.
steps.memory_tip: a is always the SQUARE ROOT of the constant left over after completing the square.

steps.label: State the standard Tan⁻¹ formula
steps.why: This is a standard, memorised result — every completing-the-square integral in this chapter ends by quoting one of the three standard forms (this one, the log form, or the Sin⁻¹ form).
common_mistakes: Confusing this with the log-form standard integral ∩dx/(x²−a²), which is used for a DIFFERENCE of squares, not a sum.
Writing Tan⁻¹ with the argument as a/x instead of x/a.
steps.memory_tip: Check the sign in the denominator: x² PLUS a² uses the Tan⁻¹ formula; x² MINUS a² uses the log formula.

steps.label: Substitute and simplify
steps.why: Substituting x → (x+1/2) and a = √3/2 directly into the standard formula's 1/a and x/a slots gives the answer in terms of (x+1/2); the /2's inside the Tan⁻¹ argument still need clearing.
common_mistakes: Substituting only in the Tan⁻¹ argument and forgetting to also replace 1/a with 2/√3 in front.
Leaving the answer as 1/(√3/2) without simplifying it to 2/√3.
steps.memory_tip: 1 divided by a fraction flips it — 1/(√3/2) = 2/√3, used twice in this line.

steps.label: Final answer
steps.why: Multiplying the numerator and denominator of (x+1/2)/(√3/2) by 2 clears the internal fractions, turning it into the tidy (2x+1)/√3 that examiners expect in the final line.
common_mistakes: Leaving the Tan⁻¹ argument as the un-simplified (x+1/2)/(√3/2) instead of clearing it to (2x+1)/√3.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply top and bottom of the inner fraction by 2 to clear the halves in one clean move.
